title: Invertible maps and isomorphic spaces
objectives: Prove that two finite-dimensional spaces are isomorphic exactly when they have the same dimension.

screens.title: Bootstrapping a curve
screens.prose: Three bonds pay the cash flows in the rows of $\mathbf{C}$, in years 1 to 3. They cost £101.85, £103.55 and £105.10. A discount factor $d_k$ is today's price of £1 paid in year $k$, so $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{d}$ gives the prices. Solve from the top down.
screens.question: Find $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_3$.

hints.text: Bond 1 has one cash flow: $d_1 = 101.85 / 105$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve bond 1 first, then use each answer in the next bond.

byKey.coupon3: You divided the whole price by 105. First take off the two coupons, £4.85 and £4.70.

screens.title: A bond too many
screens.prose: Replace bond 3 by a bond paying $(10, 210, 0)$: exactly twice bond 2, priced at £207.10. Move each slider and watch the model prices.
screens.question: Which discount factor do the three prices fail to pin down?

options.text: $d_3$: no bond pays in year 3 any more

options.why: Move $d_1$: every model price changes. Bond 1 still fixes it at 0.97.
Move $d_2$: bonds 2 and 3 change. Bond 2 still fixes it at 0.94.

options.text: None: three bonds fix three factors
options.why: Move $d_3$: no price moves. The third bond repeats the second.

hints.text: Move $d_3$ alone.
No model price depends on $d_3$.
The new bond is twice bond 2, so it adds no equation: the rank is 2.

feedback.correct: Right. The third column is zero, so $d_3$ is free.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move each slider in turn and see which one changes no price.

explain.text: The new bond's row is twice bond 2's, so $\mathbf{C}'$ has rank 2. Its third column is zero, so $\mathbf{C}'(0, 0, 1) = \mathbf{0}$ and $d_3$ never shows in a price. The map $\mathbf{d} \mapsto \mathbf{C}'\mathbf{d}$ is not injective, so it cannot be undone.

screens.title: Invertible maps
screens.prose: $T \in \mathcal{L}(V, W)$ is **invertible** when some $S \in \mathcal{L}(W, V)$ has $ST = I_V$ and $TS = I_W$. Such an $S$ is an **inverse**. An invertible linear map is an **isomorphism**, and $V$ and $W$ are then **isomorphic**, $V \cong W$. First: there is only one inverse.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $S_1$ and $S_2$ are both inverses of $T$.
$S_1 = S_1I_W = S_1(TS_2)$, since $TS_2 = I_W$.
$= (S_1T)S_2 = I_VS_2 = S_2$, as composition is associative and $S_1T = I_V$.
So the inverse is unique; we write it $T^{-1}$. $\blacksquare$
$S_1$ and $S_2$ agree on a basis, so $S_1 = S_2$.
lines.why: Nothing yet says they agree on any vector. Use $TS_2 = I_W$ and $S_1T = I_V$.

hints.text: Sandwich: $S_1 = S_1 I_W$.
Replace $I_W$ by $TS_2$, then regroup.

feedback.correct: Right. Associativity moves the brackets, and each identity does its part.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from $S_1 = S_1I_W$ and regroup.

byKey.x1: You assumed the two maps agree somewhere. The proof must produce that from the two identities.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: $S_1 = S_1(TS_2) = (S_1T)S_2 = S_2$. Only associativity and the two identities were used. So we may speak of the inverse $T^{-1}$, as for matrices in `vectors` l10.

screens.title: The inverse is linear
screens.prose: Suppose only that $T$ is linear and has an inverse function $T^{-1}$. Prove that $T^{-1}$ is linear too.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $\mathbf{w}_1, \mathbf{w}_2 \in W$.
$T(T^{-1}\mathbf{w}_1 + T^{-1}\mathbf{w}_2) = \mathbf{w}_1 + \mathbf{w}_2$, as $T$ is linear and $TT^{-1} = I_W$.
Apply $T^{-1}$: $T^{-1}\mathbf{w}_1 + T^{-1}\mathbf{w}_2 = T^{-1}(\mathbf{w}_1 + \mathbf{w}_2)$.
Likewise $T(\lambda T^{-1}\mathbf{w}) = \lambda\mathbf{w}$ gives $T^{-1}(\lambda\mathbf{w}) = \lambda T^{-1}\mathbf{w}$. $\blacksquare$
$T^{-1}$ is the inverse matrix, and matrix multiplication is linear.
lines.why: $T$ may act on polynomials, with no matrix chosen. Use only $T$ and $T^{-1}$.

hints.text: Apply $T$ to $T^{-1}\mathbf{w}_1 + T^{-1}\mathbf{w}_2$.
Linearity of $T$ and $TT^{-1} = I_W$ give $\mathbf{w}_1 + \mathbf{w}_2$.
Then apply $T^{-1}$ to both sides, and repeat for scaling.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $T$ of the sum, then undo it with $T^{-1}$.

byKey.x1: You assumed a matrix. The proof works for any linear map, matrix or not.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: $T$ sends $T^{-1}\mathbf{w}_1 + T^{-1}\mathbf{w}_2$ to $\mathbf{w}_1 + \mathbf{w}_2$. Applying $T^{-1}$ shows $T^{-1}$ keeps sums, and scaling goes the same way. So an isomorphism's inverse is an isomorphism.

screens.title: When an inverse exists
screens.prose: Invertible maps are injective and surjective (quiz). Conversely, suppose $T$ is injective and surjective. Define $S\mathbf{w}$ to be the $\mathbf{v}$ with $T\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{w}$.
screens.question: Why does this define $S\mathbf{w}$ for every $\mathbf{w} \in W$?

options.text: Surjective gives at least one such $\mathbf{v}$, and injective gives at most one.
Injective gives exactly one for each $\mathbf{w}$.
options.why: Injective gives at most one. $(x, y) \mapsto (x, y, 0)$ has none for $(0, 0, 1)$.

options.text: Surjective gives exactly one for each $\mathbf{w}$.
options.why: Surjective gives at least one. $(x + y, y + z)$ has a whole line for each $\mathbf{w}$.

options.text: $T$ is linear.
options.why: Linearity alone gives neither: the zero map is linear.

hints.text: A definition needs one answer, no more and no fewer.
Which property rules out none? Which rules out two?
Surjective: at least one. Injective: at most one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask separately why there is a $\mathbf{v}$, and why only one.

explain.text: Surjective means every $\mathbf{w}$ has a preimage, and injective means it has only one. So $S$ is a function with $TS = I_W$ and $ST = I_V$. The last screen's proof then makes $S$ linear.

screens.title: Isomorphic means equal dimension
screens.prose: Axler 3.59: finite-dimensional $V$ and $W$ are isomorphic exactly when $\dim V = \dim W$. First the forward direction, by rank-nullity.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $T : V \to W$ be an isomorphism.
$T$ is injective, so $\ker T = \{\mathbf{0}\}$ (l6).
$T$ is surjective, so $\operatorname{im} T = W$.
Rank-nullity: $\dim V = \dim \ker T + \dim \operatorname{im} T = 0 + \dim W$. $\blacksquare$
$V$ and $W$ have the same number of vectors, so $\dim V = \dim W$.
lines.why: Both hold infinitely many vectors. Dimension counts a basis, not the vectors.

hints.text: An isomorphism is injective and surjective.
Translate each into a fact about $\ker T$ or $\operatorname{im} T$.
Then add them with rank-nullity.

feedback.correct: Right. Nullity 0 and rank $\dim W$ give $\dim V = \dim W$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\dim \ker T$ and $\dim \operatorname{im} T$, then use rank-nullity.

byKey.x1: You counted vectors. A space over $\mathbb{R}$ has infinitely many; count a basis instead.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Injective gives nullity 0, and surjective gives rank $\dim W$. Rank-nullity adds them to $\dim V$. So isomorphic spaces have equal dimension.

screens.title: Equal dimension gives an isomorphism
screens.prose: Now suppose $\dim V = \dim W = n$. Build the isomorphism from two bases.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $(\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n)$ and $(\mathbf{w}_1, \dots, \mathbf{w}_n)$ be bases of $V$ and $W$.
By the linear map lemma (l5), some linear $T$ has $T\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{w}_k$.
Surjective: any $\mathbf{w} = \sum c_k\mathbf{w}_k$ is $T(\sum c_k\mathbf{v}_k)$, as the $\mathbf{w}_k$ span $W$.
Injective: $T(\sum c_k\mathbf{v}_k) = \sum c_k\mathbf{w}_k = \mathbf{0}$ forces every $c_k = 0$, as the $\mathbf{w}_k$ are independent.
So $T$ is injective and surjective: an isomorphism. $\blacksquare$
Injective: the $\mathbf{v}_k$ are independent, and $T$ keeps independence.
lines.why: Not every linear map keeps independence: $D$ sends $(1, x)$ to $(0, 1)$. Use the $\mathbf{w}_k$.

hints.text: Pick bases of the same length.
Send each $\mathbf{v}_k$ to $\mathbf{w}_k$ by the lemma.
Bases; lemma; surjective and injective (either order); conclude.

feedback.correct: Right. Basis to basis gives an isomorphism.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Define $T$ on a basis, then check each property using the $\mathbf{w}_k$.

byKey.x1: You let $T$ keep independence. That fails for maps with a kernel; here it is the $\mathbf{w}_k$ that are independent.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: The lemma sends a basis of $V$ to a basis of $W$. Spanning of the $\mathbf{w}_k$ gives surjective, and their independence gives injective. So $\mathcal{P}_3(\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}^4$ by coordinates, and $\mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2} \cong \mathbb{R}^4$.

screens.title: One property is enough
screens.prose: The first three spaces are isomorphic to each other. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^3, \mathbb{R}^2)$ matches $\mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}$ by the matrix, so its dimension is 6. Take a linear $T : \mathcal{P}_3(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$ that is injective.
screens.question: Is $T$ an isomorphism?

options.text: Yes: $\dim \operatorname{im} T = 4 - 0 = 4$, so $\operatorname{im} T = \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$.
Not yet: we must also check it is surjective.
options.why: With equal dimensions, rank-nullity does that check for us.

options.text: No: polynomials and matrices are different objects.
options.why: Isomorphic spaces may hold different objects. Only the dimension matters.

options.text: Yes: every linear map between spaces of dimension 4 is one.
options.why: The zero map is not. Here injectivity is what makes it work.

hints.text: Use rank-nullity with nullity 0.
The rank is 4, the dimension of $\mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$.
A subspace of full dimension is the whole space (l4), so $T$ is onto.

feedback.correct: Right. With equal dimensions, injective, surjective and invertible coincide.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the rank from rank-nullity.

explain.text: Nullity 0 gives rank 4, and an independent list of length 4 in $\mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$ is a basis (l4). So $\operatorname{im} T$ is everything. When $\dim V = \dim W$, any one of injective, surjective, invertible gives the other two.

screens.title: Injective is not enough
screens.prose: A classmate says $T(x, y) = (x, y, 0)$ is injective, so it is an isomorphism from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^3$. The plane is $\operatorname{im} T$, the plane $z = 0$.
screens.question: Is $T$ an isomorphism onto $\mathbb{R}^3$?

options.text: No: it is not surjective, since $\mathbf{e}_3$ is never reached.
Yes: an injective linear map is an isomorphism.
options.why: Only when the dimensions match. Here $\dim \operatorname{im} T = 2 < 3$.

options.text: Yes: $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the plane $z = 0$ look the same.
options.why: That is an isomorphism onto the plane, not onto $\mathbb{R}^3$.

options.text: No: it is not injective.
options.why: It is injective: $(x, y, 0) = \mathbf{0}$ forces $x = y = 0$.

hints.text: Is every vector of $\mathbb{R}^3$ an output?
Every output has third entry 0.
$\mathbf{e}_3 = (0, 0, 1)$ is not reached, so $T$ is not surjective.

feedback.correct: Right. Injective but not surjective, so not invertible.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a vector of $\mathbb{R}^3$ that $T$ never reaches.

byKey.inj: You treated injective as enough. That needs $\dim V = \dim W$, and $2 \ne 3$.

explain.text: Every output has $z = 0$, so the image is the plane and $\mathbf{e}_3$ lies off it. Rank-nullity agrees: rank $2 < 3$. By Axler 3.59, $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ are not isomorphic at all.

screens.title: Infinite dimension
screens.prose: $M$ on $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$, all polynomials, multiplies by $x$: $Mp = xp$. It is linear. Rank-nullity needs a finite-dimensional space, and $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$ is not one.
screens.question: Which is true of $M$?

options.text: Injective but not surjective: 1 is not $x$ times any polynomial.
Surjective: every polynomial is a multiple of $x$.
options.why: Not 1: every $xp$ vanishes at 0, as the dot shows.

options.text: Not injective: $x \cdot 0 = 0$.
options.why: That shows only $0 \in \ker M$. $xp = 0$ forces $p = 0$.

options.text: Invertible, with inverse $p \mapsto p/x$.
options.why: $p/x$ is not a polynomial when $p(0) \ne 0$, as for $1 + x$.

hints.text: Every output $xp$ has a value at $x = 0$. What is it?
$xp$ vanishes at 0, so 1 is never an output.
$xp = 0$ forces $p = 0$, so $M$ is injective. It is not surjective.

feedback.correct: Right. Injective, not surjective: rank-nullity has no grip here.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check $\ker M$, then ask whether 1 is an output.

explain.text: $xp = 0$ forces $p = 0$, so $\ker M = \{0\}$. But every $xp$ vanishes at 0, so 1 is not in the image. In finite dimension this cannot happen to an operator; in infinite dimension it can.

screens.title: Invert only an isomorphism
screens.prose: The starter decides invertibility by a small determinant. But $0.1\mathbf{I}$ of size 10 has determinant $10^{-10}$, while its condition number is 1 and `matrix_rank` gives 10: it is perfectly invertible. A determinant scales with every entry; rank does not.
screens.question: Fix `invert_if_iso(A)`: return the inverse, rounded to 6 places, when $\mathbf{A}$ is square of full rank, else `None`.

tests.call: invert_if_iso(0.1 * np.eye(10)) == [[10.0 if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(10)] for i in range(10)]

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. They cover the bond inverse within 0.000001, three non-isomorphisms, $0.1\mathbf{I}$ and a $2 \times 2$ case. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: A non-square matrix is never an isomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Replace the determinant test by `np.linalg.matrix_rank(A) < n`.
Check the shape first, then the rank, then invert.

feedback.correct: Right. Shape and rank decide it, not the size of the determinant.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Read the first failing row: the non-square case, or $0.1\mathbf{I}$?

byKey.test-5: $0.1\mathbf{I}$ has determinant $10^{-10}$ but full rank. Test the rank, not the determinant.
byKey.test-3: A $2 \times 3$ matrix has no determinant. Check the shape before anything else.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. `np.linalg.det` fails on a non-square matrix.

explain.text:
Invertible means square with full rank, by Axler 3.59 and rank-nullity. The determinant of $0.1\mathbf{I}$ is $0.1^{10} = 10^{-10}$, tiny though nothing is wrong. Rank and condition number ignore that uniform scale.

```python
if np.linalg.matrix_rank(A) < n:
    return None
```

screens.title: A curve needs enough bonds
screens.prose: With $\mathbf{C}$, bootstrapping inverts an isomorphism from discount factors to prices. With $\mathbf{C}'$ the map has rank 2. Every curve $\mathbf{d}$ with $\mathbf{C}'\mathbf{d} = (101.85, 103.55, 207.10)$ prices all three bonds correctly.
screens.question: What is the dimension of the set of such curves, $\mathbf{d}_p + \ker \mathbf{C}'$?

hints.text: Rank-nullity for $\mathbf{C}'$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$.
Rank 2, so nullity $3 - 2 = 1$.
$\ker \mathbf{C}' = \operatorname{span}\{(0, 0, 1)\}$: $d_3$ is free.

feedback.correct: Right. A line of curves: $(0.97, 0.94, t)$ for any $t$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use rank-nullity: the solutions form a copy of the kernel.

byKey.unique: You expected one curve. That needs an injective map, and $\mathbf{C}'(0, 0, 1) = \mathbf{0}$.
byKey.rank: You gave the rank. The free directions are the nullity, $3 - 2$.
byKey.all: You counted every discount factor. Two of them are pinned down.

explain.text: The kernel of $\mathbf{C}'$ is spanned by $(0, 0, 1)$, so the consistent curves are $(0.97, 0.94, t)$. Three-year money has no price. A curve needs as many independent instruments as nodes, so that the pricing map is an isomorphism.

ideas: An isomorphism is an invertible linear map. Its inverse is unique and linear, and invertible means injective and surjective.
Finite-dimensional spaces are isomorphic exactly when they have the same dimension (Axler 3.59).
When $\dim V = \dim W$, injective, surjective and invertible are the same, by rank-nullity. In infinite dimension they part ways.
summary.trap: Injective is not enough when the dimensions differ: $(x, y) \mapsto (x, y, 0)$ misses $\mathbf{e}_3$.

quiz.prose: Show that an invertible $T$ is injective.
quiz.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $T$ is invertible and $T\mathbf{u} = T\mathbf{v}$.
Apply $T^{-1}$: $T^{-1}T\mathbf{u} = T^{-1}T\mathbf{v}$.
$T^{-1}T = I_V$, so $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}$. $\blacksquare$
$T\mathbf{u} = T\mathbf{v}$ means $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}$, by definition.
lines.why: That is the definition of injective, which is what we must prove.

feedback.correct: Right. $T^{-1}$ undoes $T$, so equal images have equal inputs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply $T^{-1}$ to both sides.

byKey.x1: You assumed the conclusion. Use $T^{-1}T = I_V$ instead.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Applying $T^{-1}$ to $T\mathbf{u} = T\mathbf{v}$ gives $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}$. Surjective is similar: $\mathbf{w} = T(T^{-1}\mathbf{w})$. So every invertible map is injective and surjective.

quiz.prose: $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^3, \mathbb{R}^2)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}$, by taking matrices.
quiz.question: What is $\dim \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^3, \mathbb{R}^2)$?

feedback.correct: Right. $2 \times 3 = 6$ entries, one basis map each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the entries of a $2 \times 3$ matrix.

byKey.add: You added the dimensions. A map is a $2 \times 3$ matrix, with $2 \times 3$ entries.
byKey.sq: You used $3 \times 3$. The codomain $\mathbb{R}^2$ gives 2 rows.

explain.text: A linear map $\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is fixed by its $2 \times 3$ matrix, and every matrix gives one. So the space is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}$, of dimension 6. In general $\dim \mathcal{L}(V, W) = \dim V \cdot \dim W$.

quiz.prose: Axler 3.59 sorts finite-dimensional spaces by dimension.
quiz.question: Which space is isomorphic to $\mathcal{P}_3(\mathbb{R})$?

options.text: $\mathbb{R}^4$
$\mathbb{R}^3$
options.why: You counted the degree. $\mathcal{P}_3$ has the four basis vectors $1, x, x^2, x^3$.

options.text: $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$
options.why: All polynomials form an infinite-dimensional space.

options.text: $\mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}$
options.why: That has dimension 6.

explain.text: $\dim \mathcal{P}_3 = 4$, so $\mathcal{P}_3 \cong \mathbb{R}^4$. The map $a + bx + cx^2 + dx^3 \mapsto (a, b, c, d)$ is an isomorphism. It is the coordinate map of l4.

quiz.prose: In the backward direction of Axler 3.59, $T(\sum c_k\mathbf{v}_k) = \sum c_k\mathbf{w}_k = \mathbf{0}$.
quiz.question: Why does this force every $c_k = 0$?

options.text: The $\mathbf{w}_k$ are a basis of $W$, so they are independent.
The $\mathbf{v}_k$ are independent.
options.why: The equation is a combination of the $\mathbf{w}_k$, in $W$.

options.text: $T$ is injective.
options.why: That is what this step proves. Using it is circular.

options.text: $\dim V = \dim W$.
options.why: Equal dimension made the bases the same length. The zero conclusion needs independence.

feedback.correct: Right. Independence of the $\mathbf{w}_k$ does it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which list appears in $\sum c_k\mathbf{w}_k = \mathbf{0}$?

explain.text: $\sum c_k\mathbf{w}_k = \mathbf{0}$ is a zero combination of the $\mathbf{w}_k$. They form a basis, so they are independent and every $c_k = 0$. So $\ker T = \{\mathbf{0}\}$.
